newsitem.title: FRANCE: GAN has no comment on new state cash call.
newsitem.headline: GAN has no comment on new state cash call.

text.p: French state insurer GAN had no comment on Monday on a newspaper report that it would tell the government in January it would need seven to 10 billion francs ($1.3-$1.9 billion) in fresh state aid before it could be privatised.
"We have no comment on the subject," said a spokeswoman. "As far as I know no timetable (for talking to the government) has been set," she added.
Business daily Les Echos said that according to various estimates, the recapitalisation needed to prepare the insurer for privatisation would be 7-10 billion francs.

GAN's former chairman, Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, said in November that GAN would need to go to the government for more money before being sold despite receiving a 2.8 billion franc recapitalisation from the state in 1995.
At the time, he was unwilling to estimate the amount, but he said last year, before GAN received the money, that the group could need 7-10 billion francs.
Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN), which was hammered by a slump in French property values, is the lone French composite insurer still in state hands.

The newspaper said some four billion francs would be needed to increase provisions on GAN's two ring-fenced defeasance companies Baticredit and Parixel, whose non-performing property loans total 16.5 billion francs and are currently provisioned at 52.5 percent.
Its property financing arm UIC which had a first half loss of 758 million francs could post a three billion franc loss for the full year, the newspaper said.
Such a loss would require a capital injection of three billion francs to maintain GAN's solvency ratios, it said.

Bonnaud was fired by the government in November and replaced by Didier Pfeiffer after plans to privatise its regional banking network CIC, France's fifth largest commercial bank, ended in failure with just one eligible bid submitted.

The government has said it is determined to press ahead with selling CIC. But its sale at anything less than the 14.5 billion francs at which it is held in the insurer's accounts would mean a capital loss that would increase GAN's recapitalisation needs.
Bonnaud said in November that GAN's full year loss was likely to nearly double its half year loss of 965 million francs, due to losses connected with its past property financing activities.
But he said that with fresh state capital, privatisation of the group remained a "realistic" possiblity in 1997.
Last week, GAN named Bankers Trust to study sale of part of Baticredit's distressed property loan portfolio.
